The rule

Mastery learning is one rule: you don't move on until you can show you've got it. Bloom, an education researcher at the University of Chicago, proposed it in 1968. Teach a unit, test it, fix exactly what each student missed, test again, and only then go on.

The experiment

Two of his doctoral students, Joanne Anania and Arthur Burke, put it to the test. They randomly assigned school students to three ways of learning the same material: a conventional class of about thirty, a class of thirty taught with mastery learning, and a good tutor for each student, also with mastery learning.

The result

The mastery class finished one standard deviation ahead of the conventional class. The tutored students finished two standard deviations ahead, and about nine in ten of them reached a level that only the top fifth of the conventional class did.

Bloom called it a problem because a tutor for every student was, he wrote, “too costly for most societies to bear on a large scale”. Now it isn't.
